options.title: How a Hiding Man Became Emperor of Rome
options.description: In 41 AD, Claudius was found hiding behind a curtain in the imperial palace following Caligula's death. The Praetorian Guard declared him Emperor. Sources: Suetonius (Life of Claudius), Josephus (Antiquities of the Jews).
script_lines: In forty-one AD, a terrified middle-aged man hid behind a palace curtain, convinced he was about to be executed.
Hours after the assassination of Emperor Caligula, nervous soldiers swarmed the imperial palace quarters searching for remaining family members.
A guard named Gratus noticed two feet peeking out beneath a heavy textile drapery and yanked the fabric aside.
Instead of drawing a sword, the soldier recognized fifty-year-old Claudius, fell to one knee, and hailed him as Caesar.
Claudius, who had spent his entire life mocked for his limp and stammer, was carried to the Praetorian camp on a litter.
The guard unit effectively secured his loyalty with a massive financial bonus, establishing a pattern where soldiers selected the ruler of Rome.

options.title: When Julius Caesar Demanded a Higher Ransom
options.description: In 75 BC, young Julius Caesar was captured by Cilician pirates. He insisted they double his ransom demands and bossed them around until released. Sources: Plutarch (Life of Caesar), Suetonius.
script_lines: When Mediterranean pirates kidnapped twenty-five-year-old Julius Caesar, he insulted their math and demanded they double his ransom.
Off the coast of Pharmacusa, pirates captured the young noble and demanded twenty talents of silver for his safe release.
Caesar laughed in their faces, claiming he was worth at least fifty talents, and sent his servants to gather the higher sum.
For nearly thirty-eight days, he treated his captors like subordinates, writing speeches and forcing the pirates to listen.
Whenever they failed to admire his poetry, he openly warned them that he would return with a fleet to capture them all.
The pirates treated his threats as a joke until the ransom arrived, after which Caesar raised a navy and tracked down their camp.

options.title: The Origin of the Line in the Sand
options.description: In 168 BC, Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas drew a circle in the dirt around King Antiochus IV, forcing a peace decision on the spot. Sources: Polybius (Histories 29.27), Livy (Ab Urbe Condita 45.12).
script_lines: The phrase drawing a line in the sand began with one audacious Roman diplomat facing down an invading King.
In one hundred sixty-eight BC, King Antiochus the Fourth marched his Seleucid army into Egypt, preparing to take Alexandria.
A single Roman envoy named Gaius Popillius Laenas met the king outside the city, holding only a simple wooden staff.
When Antiochus offered a friendly greeting, Popillius handed over a Senate decree demanding an immediate military retreat.
The king asked for time to consult his councilors, but Popillius drew a circle in the dirt around the monarch's feet.
He told the king to give his answer before stepping across the line, forcing Antiochus to yield to Rome without drawing a sword.
